newsitem.title: USA: San Francisco votes on $525 mln stadium plan.
newsitem.headline: San Francisco votes on $525 mln stadium plan.

text.p: Voters headed to the polls here Tuesday to decide the fate of a proposed $525 million stadium-mall complex, capping a heated and sometimes raunchy election campaign.

Stories about the stadium plan have been splashed across the city's newspapers for several months, but San Francisco's registrar of voters has predicted a turnout of only 30 percent of the city's 411,000 registered voters.
At the polls, voters will consider two stadium-related measures, both requiring a majority vote of support to pass.

Proposition D would authorize the sale of up to $100 million of lease revenue bonds to finance the city's share of the proposed San Francisco 49ers stadium and shopping complex. Proposition F would waive certain zoning restrictions for the project to expedite construction.
Recent voter polls suggest the stadium ballot measures have made little headway with voters despite the aggressive campaign mounted by team owners and Mayor Willie Brown.

The stadium measures trailed by nine percentage points in one recent San Francisco Chronicle newspaper poll. A San Francisco KPIX-TV and KCBS radio poll also showed the stadium measure trailing, but by only four percentage points.

Despite the polls and low voter turnout projections, stadium-backers said they were confident. "It looks really good for us," campaign spokesman Michael Colbruno said. "We are turning out our people."
San Francisco's heated stadium campaign pit Mayor Brown, a flamboyant and popular figure, against state Senator Quentin Kopp, one of the area's most powerful and outspoken lawmakers.

Stadium supporters have argued that the stadium-mall project would generate hundreds of millions of dollars each year in economic activity for San Francisco and create thousands of jobs for one of the city's poorest neighborhoods.

Stadium opponents said the project was a form of "corporate welfare" because it would put San Francisco's budget on the line to benefit wealthy team owners. "Is San Francisco wearing a 'Kick Me' sign?", the campaign against the stadium said in the city's voter guide.

Hoping to allay fears the stadium plan could hurt the city's budget, Brown unveiled a financial plan that he said would guarantee the city would never have to dip into its general fund to pay off the bonds for the project.
The plan, structured by Morgan Stanley Group Inc, would include bond insurance by Financial Security Assurance, a unit of Financial Security Assurance Holdings Ltd.
Kopp presented his own financial plan last week, proposing a surcharge on ticket sales to pay for a portion of the project and protect the city's general fund.
Although San Francisco's stadium debate has been focused on the fiscal issues of bonding and zoning, the campaign has had its raunchy side.

Last month, stadium supporters were dealt a bizarre public-relations setback when friends threw a wild party to celebrate the 50th birthday of Jack Davis, one of San Francisco's most powerful political consultants who is managing the campaign for the 49ers stadium plan.
The private party, which featured live sex acts, strippers and sadomasochism, stunned one of the world's most tolerant cities and sent shockwaves through its political elite.
Controversy over the party, attended by many of the city's power brokers, snowballed, leading some to believe it could undermine public support for the stadium.
